newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Barefoot N.Korean woman crosses border to South.
newsitem.headline: Barefoot N.Korean woman crosses border to South.

text.p: A North Korean woman fled barefoot through minefields and razor wire barriers to South Korea on Thursday, but Seoul reported no progress in talks aimed at letting a top Pyongyang defector in China gain asylum in the South.

The South Korean Defence Ministry said the woman in her 20s had reached the South after a perilous crossing of the eastern sector of the heavily-guarded demilitarised zone (DMZ) bisecting the Korean peninsula.
"She was barefoot and wearing a black jumper but we will not release any more details on her as we have to protect North Korean defectors," a ministry spokesman said.
The ministry declined to say how she had managed to elude heavy concentrations of communist troops guarding one of the world's tensest frontiers.

The four-km (2.5 mile) wide DMZ was created as a buffer zone between the rival states under the 1953 truce agreement which ended the Korean War, but the zone, sealed off from the public by barbed wire, has since been sown with thousands of mines. Both sides have installed many advanced weapons there.
The Defence Ministry refused to confirm a report by KBS state radio which identified the woman as Li Ju-son, 25.

It said she was found near a South Korean guard post at the Cold War frontier and told the military that she wanted to escape poverty in her homeland, which is threatened with famine after floods destroyed grain harvests two years in a row.

Southern troops fed the exhausted woman after she had complained of hunger, it added. Her defection coincided with the funeral of defector Li Il-nam who was shot earlier this month by two suspected North Korean gunmen just south of Seoul.
"After the shooting incident in which a North Korean defector was fatally wounded, we have decided not to release personal details of defectors," the ministry spokesman said.
The young woman's motives for fleeing were being investigated, he said. She left behind her mother and a sister.

Seoul Foreign Ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung said he believed the woman's defection would not affect talks between South Korea and China over the fate of Hwang Jang-yop, the most senior official yet to flee North Korea.
Hwang has been holed up at South Korea's consular office in Beijing since seeking asylum there with an aide on Febuary 12.

"Today's incident is just the latest of a string of defections by North Koreans," Lee said. "She is not a senior figure in the North and I don't see any reason why this will have any impact on our talks in Beijing."
The Hwang talks resumed on Wednesday after being suspended following the death last week of Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping.
"It appears that China has not made a decision yet," Lee said. In Beijing, South Korean embassy spokesman Chang Moon-ik said he did not expect Hwang to leave China in February.
Lee said he believed Chinese authorities were anxious not to offend Pyongyang, its old communist ally, but would eventually allow Hwang, North Korea's chief ideologue, to come to Seoul.

His defection placed further strain on ties between the two Koreas, which had just begun to reopen contacts frozen after a North Korean submarine dropped 26 intruders on a Southern beach last September.
Three days after Hwang sought asylum in Beijing, defector Li Il-nam was shot in the head outside a friend's flat near Seoul. Li, known in the South as Lee Han-yong, died on Tuesday.
South Korean police said on Thursday that Li's friend had received a letter threatening him and his wife for cooperating with police probing the shooting.
"The letter said the couple would face retaliation if they cooperated with our investigation and their apartment would be blown up," police spokesman Ha Seung-gyun said by telephone.
Police are working on the theory that Pyongyang instructed its agents to murder Li as a warning to South Korea and other North Korean escapees following Hwang's defection.

South Korean police have virtually ruled out earlier suspicions that Lee might have been gunned down by loan sharks or underworld hitmen. Li, who was the nephew of Pyongyang leader Kim Jong-il's ex-wife, ran into financial trouble after he defected to the South in 1982 and went into business.
